messages.subject: [statnet_help] problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Muriel.  Sorry for the long delay.

When I first looked at your code I noticed that you are not passing a  
"decay" argument to the gwidegree and gwodegree terms and I thought  
this might be causing a problem (since this argument is supposed to be  
required!), but now that I've had a chance to look more carefully and  
run part of your code, it seems that it is proceeding just fine with  
the default value of zero.

There is definitely a problem with these lines:
#variabelen in matrix-bestanden plakken
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"klasnr2",attx)
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"OndType",attx)
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"female",attx)
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"alloch2b",attx)

In each one, you should be using the individual column from attx  
instead of attx itself, as in:
#variabelen in matrix-bestanden plakken
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"klasnr2",klasnr2)
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"OndType",OndType)
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"female",female)
set.vertex.attribute(co.matw1,"alloch2b",alloch2b)

Your original code is resulting in some bizarre behavior I don't yet  
understand and will need to look into further:  Somehow it created  
vertex attributes of length 20164 (even though attx has only 852  
elements total).  Given that your model does use nodematch with these  
vertex attributes, these very-long attributes could be causing part of  
the trouble you're seeing.

That said, I would also be curious about two things regarding the  
gwidegree and gwodegree terms:  (1) Have you updated your version of  
ergm recently from CRAN?  There used to be a bug with either gwodegree  
or gwidegree, I can't remember which, but we fixed that.  (2) See what  
happens if you set the decay value by hand and use the fixed=TRUE  
option.  (e.g., gwidegree(0.2, fixed=TRUE)).  If that seems to work  
okay, then see if you can get fixed=FALSE to work, but doing this  
creates a much larger computational burden.

Hope this helps.
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interpreting GWESP
messages.body_plain:
greetings,

i am wondering if there is a straightforward formula that can be used to 
interpret the GWESP coefficient, together with the weight parameter, in 
more commonsense language? in other words, i am looking for a way to 
interpret the coefficient in a manner that is comparable to the other 
terms in the model, by saying, for instance, that if a tie closes a 
SINGLE triangle, then the log-odds of that tie forming increases by X, 
if a tie closes only TWO triangles, then the log-odds of that tie 
forming increases by Y, etc etc (thus, i would be able to directly 
compare the likelihood of such ties to, say, a tie that symmetrizes a 
dyad or a tie that is racially homophilous). is there an easy way to 
determine such log-odds, then, as a function of a) the coefficient, b) 
the weight parameter, and c) the number of triangles that the tie will 
form? (as goodreau et al. do in 'birds of a feather,' i think- hunter 
2007 also includes something comparable.)

thanks greatly!

-kevin

-- 
Kevin Lewis
Ph.D. Candidate in Sociology
Harvard University
641 William James Hall
33 Kirkland Street
Cambridge, MA 02138

Best regards,

Jichao Qian

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interpreting GWESP
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

A wonderful question.  Interpretation of GWESP can be complex and subtle - 
every time I work with it for a sustained period, I find new ways of 
thinking about it.  At some point, if I ever find the time (ha!) I'd love 
to write it all out (along with my thoughts on GWDSP and perhaps GWD) into 
a paper.

In the meanwhile, it's important to note that the interpretation is not as 
straightforward as you lay out. The number of triangles that the edge will 
close matters, so one component of the change in log-odds involves this. 
But one needs to think of things from the point of view of the other two 
ties in each of those triangles that will be close.  The number of 
triangles that each of them is in will also change, and that will affect 
the log-odds of the first tie as well.  Ive never sat down and put it all 
into a single formula for specifying the logodds as a function of these 
different quantities, but it shoulnd't be complicated. Unfortunately, 
it'll never be quite as straightforward as many other commonly used 
statistics.

I hope that helps!
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have an ERGM model with covariates: nodeicov, nodeocov, nodeifactor,
nodeofactor, and nodemix. The model runs well and the results make sense. I
am trying to put together a presentation of the results for an audience
composed of primarily epidemiologists who would appreciate knowing the odds
ratios corresponding to the betas. I have tried exponentiating the betas but
the results do not seem quite right.... Has anyone had experience with this?
Is there some reason I should not exponentiate to get an odds ratio in an
ERGM model? I will admit that I do not understand all of the
behind-the-scenes algorithms, but my general sense was that these models
were approximately equivalent to logistic regression models....

Thanks,
jenine

--

messages.subject: [statnet_dev] RE: [statnet_help] Degeneracy problem
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jichao,

Yes, from my own experience, I find that as a whole models do seem to be more 
likely to experience degeneracy when applied to larger networks than smaller 
ones.  I personally would only suggest selecting out subsets of your data if 
you have a valid scientific reason for doing so; otherwise I'd recommend 
thinking of degeneracy as a sign that your model is not appropriate to the 
data, and keep hunting.

The degeneracy warning that sometimes appears at the end of an ergm is a bit of 
a blunt instrument, and we're working to refine it.  A much better way to 
diagnose degeneracy at this point is to examine the MCMC diagnostics. 
Instructions for doing so, and how to interpret the resulting plots, can be 
found in Section 6 of the statnet tutorial that is now published in JSS:

http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i09

Good luck!
Steve

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] exponentiating ERGM coefficients into odds ratios?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jenine,

Yes, you're right with the interpretations you listed below: those with 
coefficients above 0 (ie implying odds ratios above 1) do imply an 
increase in probability, and vice versa.  So you have interpreted the 
effects correctly.  Just remember that when you have this many terms in a 
model, the effects are conditional on one another, and can confound 
expectation!
